title: What are insurers and MGAs actually using AI for?
description: Where AI pays first for carriers, MGAs and large agencies: ranked jobs, platforms, the state AI rules, what examiners ask, and our job-ad count.
verdict: AI informs; people decide.[^1] Of 193 auto insurers in 2022, 96 used AI to inform adjusters; none to deny claims.[^2]
Start where reading piles up: submission intake for underwriters and complex claim files for adjusters.[^3][^4]
For MGAs, clean portfolio data is becoming a condition for access to capacity.[^5] Reported MGA premium grew 12% in 2025.[^6]
Thirty jurisdictions adopted the regulators' AI bulletin.[^7] It covers vendor AI, and examiners can ask for your inventory.[^8]
Keep a named person on every claim denial. Lawsuits claiming algorithms, not reviewers, drove health denials have partly survived dismissal.[^9][^10]

headings.ranked: Where does AI pay first in insurance?
headings.buy-or-build: Should you buy AI tools or build your own?

summary: AI in insurance mostly reads and drafts: it pulls facts from submissions, claim files and policy forms so underwriters and adjusters decide faster.[^3][^1][^11] People keep the decision: state regulators apply the same standards whatever tool you use.[^12][^8] Clean data and a real human check make or break it.[^13][^9]
humanRole: Underwriters keep accept, decline and price. New York expects each adverse decision to state the information used and its source.[^14][^15]
Adjusters keep every claim denial. In the regulators' auto survey, 9 of 193 insurers used AI for claim approvals and none for denials.[^2]
MGA underwriters keep the bind decision within their authority. Carriers' AI programs should cover AI from outside firms, so expect their questions.[^8]
At large agencies, a licensed person checks anything a client sees. Verify limits, deductibles, exclusions and endorsements against the policy forms.[^16]

Senior management and the board own the AI program, with a committee from underwriting, claims, compliance and legal.[^12][^8] The bulletin lists checking AI against expert review as one way to validate it.[^8]

ranked.name: Submission intake and triage (carriers and MGAs)
ranked.why: Underwriters spend up to 40% of their time on admin and other non-core work.[^3] Only 9% of underwriting leaders use AI to read and prepare submission data to a large extent; 68% expect to in three years.[^17]
ranked.payoff: Hours from submission received to quote, and the share of submissions quoted.

ranked.name: Claim file summaries for adjusters (carriers)
ranked.why: Claims is the top AI area for auto insurers, and the main use is informing adjusters.[^2][^18] In a McKinsey case study, Aviva runs 80+ claims models and assesses complex liability 23 days faster.[^4]
ranked.payoff: Adjuster minutes per file review, and days to final payment (40.7 on average for US home claims in 2026).[^19]

ranked.name: AI inventory and examiner file (carriers)
ranked.why: Examiners can ask for your written AI program, model inventory, validation work and vendor contracts.[^8] Only 24% of insurance leaders are very confident they could pass an independent AI governance review within 90 days.[^20]
ranked.payoff: Days to produce the examiner file, and the share of AI uses inventoried.

ranked.name: Bordereaux and carrier reporting (MGAs)
ranked.why: AM Best says consistent, transparent portfolio data is becoming a condition for MGAs' access to capital.[^5] It also reports added scrutiny of MGAs as the market matures.[^21]
ranked.payoff: Days to close each bordereau (the premium and claims report to a carrier), and carrier data queries per month.

ranked.name: Fraud screening (carriers)
ranked.why: Fraud costs US consumers $308.6 billion a year, a coalition figure the NAIC cites.[^22] Among insurers the regulators surveyed, 58% in auto and 55% in home use or plan AI for it.[^18]
ranked.payoff: Hit rate of referrals to your special investigations unit, checked by customer group.

ranked.name: Policy checking and coverage comparison (large agencies)
ranked.why: Coverage form analysis is agencies' second most common AI use, at 43%.[^23] A qualified person still verifies limits, deductibles, exclusions and endorsements against the policy.[^16]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per policy check, and errors caught before the client sees the policy.

ownData.title: What are your peers hiring for?
ownData.intro: We counted US insurance job ads posted in the 30 days to 26 November 2026, by job title, in one job-ad database.[^24] An ad counts as mentioning AI if it names artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, Copilot, AI tools, AI-powered or machine learning.[^24] AI shows up in modeling jobs far more than in the front-line jobs where the admin piles up.[^24][^3]

tables.title: What do insurers use AI for, by line of business?
tables.intro: From the NAIC's surveys of larger insurers, summarised in its own journal.[^18][^11] Surveys covered insurers with $250M+ in premium or a large state market share.[^29] Auto and home left out simpler statistical models and health counted them, so compare lines with care.[^18][^29]

rules.name: NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI
rules.status: In force in 30 jurisdictions (NAIC map, 13 Nov 2026)
rules.what: You need a written AI program covering governance, risk controls and audit, scaled to the possible harm to consumers.[^12][^8] It covers vendor AI, and examiners can ask for your AI inventory, vendor contracts and testing.[^8] Recent adopters include Texas, South Carolina and North Dakota; check your state's own text.[^7]

rules.name: Colorado SB21-169 and Regulation 10-1-1
rules.status: In force: life since Nov 2023; auto and health since 15 Oct 2025
rules.what: Life, private auto and health insurers need a board-overseen framework for outside consumer data and the models that use it.[^30][^31] Commercial-only carriers and MGAs writing only commercial lines are outside its scope today.[^30] Bias-testing reports are waived until the Division adopts testing rules for each line.[^32]

rules.name: New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers must show that AI and outside data in underwriting and pricing don't discriminate unfairly, with the board responsible.[^14] You stay responsible for vendor tools, so contracts should give audit rights.[^14] Adverse-decision notices should name the information used and its source.[^15]

rules.name: California Insurance Bulletin 2022-5
rules.what: California's own guidance on bias in AI and big data; the NAIC lists it in place of the model bulletin.[^7]

rules.name: NAIC third-party data and model vendor framework
rules.what: It proposes a multi-state registry and yearly attestation for vendors of property and casualty (P&C) pricing and underwriting data and models.[^33][^34] Insurers would still own their own compliance.[^35]

watchOuts: Rubber-stamp review: a lawsuit alleges Cigna doctors denied over 300,000 payment requests at about 1.2 seconds each, and a court let it proceed.[^9][^36] Nothing is proven yet; still, log review time, sample decisions and show reviewers the evidence, not only the score.

Unequal outcomes: Black homeowners allege State Farm's claim-screening algorithms slowed and questioned their claims more; the claim survived dismissal in 2023.[^37] Test outcomes by group before and after go-live; Colorado and New York expect it for covered lines.[^30][^14]
Vendor AI treated as someone else's problem. The NAIC bulletin and New York keep you responsible for vendor models, so put audit rights and regulator cooperation in the contract.[^8][^14]

Controls you can't prove: 68% of insurance leaders say their AI controls exist, but the evidence is scattered across teams and tools.[^20] Keep one inventory entry and one evidence file per AI use, because examiners can ask for both.[^8]

Trusting a vendor's accuracy figure: score it on your own files against what your experts decided, a check the bulletin names.[^8] Data quality is insurers' second biggest AI barrier, named by 45%.[^13]

Pilots that never reach the desk: only 7% of carriers in a 2026 claims study report scalable AI success.[^38] Pilot one workflow on one team with one owner and one measure; few task-specific AI tools reach production.[^39]

faq.q: How is AI used in insurance?
faq.a: Mostly to read and draft for the people who decide.[^1][^11] In regulators' surveys, claims and fraud lead in auto and home, and underwriting leads in life.[^18] Conning names AI and data-driven underwriting among the drivers of MGA growth.[^6]

faq.q: Where should a carrier or MGA start with AI?
faq.a: With one reading-heavy workflow, such as submission intake or complex claim files.[^3][^17] Pick one with a clear before-and-after number. Add it to your AI inventory from day one, since examiners can ask for it.[^8]

faq.q: What will the examiner ask about our AI?
faq.a: Expect requests for your written AI program, your inventory of models and AI systems, and how you validate and monitor them.[^8] For vendor AI, expect requests for your due diligence, contracts and audits.[^8][^12]

faq.q: Does the NAIC AI bulletin apply to MGAs?
faq.a: It is addressed to insurers.[^12] It asks insurers to cover AI they rely on from outside firms, so carrier partners may ask an MGA about its AI.[^8] AM Best describes added scrutiny of MGAs as the market matures.[^21]

faq.q: Will AI replace insurance underwriters or adjusters?
faq.a: Nothing in the data points that way. 75% of claims professionals say AI needs human oversight.[^38] Regulators hold insurers to the same standards whatever tool helped make a decision.[^12][^8]

faq.q: Which AI rules apply to insurers in my state?
faq.a: Thirty jurisdictions have issued the NAIC AI bulletin, per its 13 Nov 2026 map.[^7] California, Colorado and New York have their own guidance or rules.[^7] The NAIC says its map doesn't confirm each state kept every element, so read your state's own text.[^7]

faq.q: What does an AI platform for a carrier or MGA cost?
faq.a: The platforms in our table publish no list price.[^25] Hi Marley, for example, sells by private offer priced per user.[^26] Budget from a scoped quote for one workflow.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the job is standard, such as submission intake or claims texting, and you have no data team.[^40] Most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases, up from 53% in 2024.[^40] MIT found vendor partnerships reached production about twice as often as internal builds.[^39][^41]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your guidelines, appetite and loss history are your edge, or you must explain every step to an examiner.[^14][^8] A thin build on your own rules also avoids lock-in while the NAIC vendor registry is still a draft.[^33] A common middle path: buy the reading step, and keep the rules and the decision log yourself.

pickElse: Your core systems can't take the AI output: fix the integration first. Legacy integration is insurers' top barrier to scaling AI, named by 50%.[^13]
You already run Guidewire or Applied: check the AI they now own, such as hx and Cytora, before adding a separate tool.[^27][^28]
Your team only needs to write and summarise faster: an enterprise plan of ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft 365 Copilot will do. Bring it into your AI program, which covers generative AI too.[^8]
Simple, high-volume claims: straight-through rules in your claims system may already do the job.[^42]

offer.heading: Which insurance workflow should you hand to AI first?
offer.body: In 30 minutes we map one workflow, such as submissions, claim files or carrier bordereaux. You leave knowing who signs off, the measure to track and what your examiner or carrier partner will ask.

reviews.notes: Retarget, 26 Nov 2026: the page read as a small-agency tool guide. Now ranks carrier, MGA and large-agency jobs, each with one measure. Cut agency tools priced by the month, the AI receptionist and the renewal-CRM tips: none leads a 40-500 person insurer to a decision. Added the examiner file as a job, since governance evidence is what COOs are asked for.

Defined bordereaux in the ranked list. Pick-something-else now covers what an operations head actually hits: core-system integration, the AI already inside Guidewire or Applied, and simple claims that rules can handle. Tool table cut to four platforms with honest 'not published' prices so it fits a phone.

MGA leaders get their own bottom-line bullet: capacity now follows clean portfolio data, with AM Best and Conning behind it. Added an FAQ on whether the NAIC bulletin reaches MGAs, worded carefully: it is addressed to insurers, who must cover outside AI. Offer now names carrier bordereaux and what a carrier partner will ask.

Head of underwriting or claims asks what the examiner will ask. Replaced a vendor's summary of the bulletin with Illinois's own copy of the text, which lists the examiner requests. Replaced a vendor-commissioned underwriter survey with Accenture's 430-executive survey. Claims payoff now has a public baseline: J.D. Power's 40.7 days to final payment.

Gets the answer in 10 seconds: title is his question and the bottom line is five short bullets. Forum quotes and AI-tool listicles are gone; every claim now rests on a regulator, a court record, a large survey or the vendor's own announcement. No case from a firm his size exists in the research, so none is claimed.
